newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan shippers fear strike may hurt U.S. talks.
newsitem.headline: Japan shippers fear strike may hurt U.S. talks.

text.p: Japanese shipping firms said on Thursday they were worried that a planned strike by Japan's port workers would make it increasingly difficult to avert U.S. sanctions on Japanese vessels.

"The port workers' strike comes at a highly sensitive time and we hope the action does not aggravate the U.S.," said a spokesman for Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd, one of the three shippers to be targeted by the U.S. sanctions.

On Wednesday two major labour unions decided to stage a 24-hour nationwide strike on March 12 to protest against pressure from the United States and the European Union for reforms of Japan's port practices.

Last week, the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC), angry at what it said were costly and discriminatory practices at Japanese ports, said it would slap a $100,000 surcharge on vessels owned or operated by Kawasaki Kisen, Mitsui O.S.K. Lines Ltd and Nippon Yusen KK each time they enter a U.S. port from abroad.
The surcharges would go into effect on April 14.
Japanese and U.S. authorities are due to meet later today, after talks on Monday failed to narrow differences, a Foreign Ministry official said.
The FMC said that if Japan moves to retaliate against U.S. lines, the level of fees on Japanese carriers would be increased proportionally.
"We hope the U.S. does not interpret the port workers' action as retaliatory action against U.S. lines," a spokesman for Nippon Yusen KK said.
Shipping industry officials have estimated the surcharges would cost the three Japanese shipping firms a combined five billion yen ($40.9 million) per year.

Workers from the two unions, the National Council of Dock Workers' Unions and the Japan Confederation of Port and Transport Workers' Unions, will also refuse to handle cargoes on Sundays from March 16 onward, union officials said.
For the past two years Japan's stevedores have been working on Sundays, but only as a temporary measure to help the port of Kobe recover from the aftermath of a strong earthquake in January 1995.
After the earthquake, ships originally destined for Kobe were diverted to other ports, which extended business to Sundays in order to handle the increased freight.
Both the EU and the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission have requested that Japanese ports operate on Sundays.
Most major ports around the world operate on Sundays and shipping industry sources said they would like ports in Japan to do the same in order to maintain a competitive edge.
Japan's ports have watched business flee to neighbouring Asian countries in recent years because of high costs and because Japanese manufacturers have been shifting production overseas.
The strike on March 12 would affect operations of container ships docking at all major ports in Japan, including Yokohama and Kobe, an official of the National Council of Dock Workers' Unions said.
